problem: The sentence says a CVOR 'rotates a loop or dipole physically'. In most CVOR installations the rotating pattern is produced electrically (the antenna itself does not move), and only some older or large-aperture designs turn the antenna mechanically. A student may take 'physically' as the definition of CVOR.
fix: A conventional VOR (CVOR) rotates its radiation pattern, either mechanically or by electronic means such as a goniometer, so the phase of the 30 Hz variable signal turns with azimuth.

problem: GNSS is placed under the hyperbolic branch whose note reads 'two stations'. GNSS measures ranges (pseudoranges) to four or more satellites; it only borrows the time-difference idea through the receiver clock offset. The note can make students think two satellites give a fix.
fix: Keep GNSS in the tree as a related case, but change the note on that branch to 'range difference between station pairs' and add a note on GNSS such as 'pseudoranges; clock offset solved as an extra unknown'.

problem: The explanation says the hyperbolas 'reduce to nearly parallel straight lines'. What actually happens on the baseline extension is that the gradient of the range difference becomes very small, so each line of position there is nearly parallel to the baseline and the two families cross at a shallow angle.
fix: Answer: there the range difference changes very slowly with position, so each line of position runs almost along the baseline extension and the two lines of position cross at a shallow cut angle; a small timing error then moves the crossing point a long way.

problem: The cross-reference 'see 5.6' is plain text, so a reader on a phone cannot jump to the satellite navigation chapter.
fix: Make it a chapter link, for example: satellite navigation reuses this geometry (see 5.6).
